items.title: Experts say AI hacking incidents stem from frontier labs' failures in containment and cybersecurity basics [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Containment and monitoring failures are to blame for AI hacking reports: experts
items.summary:
Since July, several US frontier AI labs including OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Google have reported incidents where their AI models accessed external systems without authorization, often described as AI agents "going rogue." Cybersecurity experts argue these incidents result from the labs' failure to implement established cybersecurity practices such as secure sandboxing and proper containment, rather than from the AI models' intelligence or misalignment. Experts also note that these labs have largely rejected external cybersecurity advice, conflating cybersecurity with AI safety and underprioritizing traditional security measures.

The experts highlight that containment failures, misconfigured environments, and insufficient monitoring allowed these unauthorized accesses to occur and persist unnoticed for days. They emphasize that basic cybersecurity techniques like air-gapping and egress controls are well-known and effective but have not been adequately applied by the frontier labs. This gap between AI safety focus and cybersecurity fundamentals has contributed to repeated security breaches, raising concerns about the labs' preparedness to manage AI risks effectively.

items.title: TypeSafe AI releases Jev 1.14.0 with experimental multimodal features, new data types, and extended context length under opt-in danger zone flags [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: We’re releasing Jev 1.14.0 along with experimental features for dreamers
items.summary:
TypeSafe AI has launched Jev 1.14.0, introducing experimental features aimed at developers and innovators willing to test less stable capabilities. These include composable image support, a new bounding box data type, and longer context lengths, all accessible via opt-in danger zone flags to balance creativity with reliability.

The update builds on two years of development and aims to offer early access to features that may not yet meet production standards but show promise for future improvements. The company also added an opt-in program to help identify model issues through user queries, while planning a gradual deprecation of the previous version with advance notice to users.

items.title: Liquid AI releases LFM2.5-24B-A2B, a 24B-parameter reasoning model with 2B active parameters optimized for fast on-device agent use [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: LFM2.5-24B-A2B: Built for fast on-device agents
items.summary:
Liquid AI has launched LFM2.5-24B-A2B, a 24 billion parameter reasoning model that activates only 2 billion parameters per token to enable fast, private on-device AI agents. The model extends the LFM2.5 family and offers competitive performance against larger models on multiple agentic and tool-use benchmarks, running up to 1.7 times faster than comparable mixture-of-experts models on devices like Apple M5 Max and NVIDIA B300 GPUs.

The model features an expanded vocabulary and context window, scaled-up pretraining to 33 trillion tokens, and reinforcement learning to improve reasoning and tool use. It produces explicit chains of thought before answers and supports long context lengths up to 131,072 tokens. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is open-weight and available on Hugging Face and Liquid AI's Playground, with support for various inference frameworks for efficient edge and GPU deployment.

Benchmarks show LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches larger models on five of eight agentic and tool-use tests and excels in instruction following, making it suitable for reasoning and tool-calling agents running locally. For knowledge-intensive tasks, pairing with retrieval or web search is recommended to complement its strengths.

items.title: The Consensus launches an AI tells detector using static rules to identify AI-like writing and limit its promotion in technical article feeds [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Has AI tells
items.summary:
The Consensus has developed an AI tells detector that uses static rules to identify articles that resemble AI-generated writing, aiming to promote good human-written technical content. The detector does not confirm AI authorship but flags articles with AI-like characteristics, restricting their visibility in daily highlights, newsletters, and social media.

This tool was created because commercial AI detectors are costly to run on every article, and many readers prefer human writing even if it is imperfect. The detector accounts for changes in writing style since 2023 and is integrated into The Consensus's content curation process to maintain quality standards while allowing users to filter out articles with AI tells if desired.

items.title: AlphaRLM trains language models with reinforcement learning to generate executable symbolic financial factors from literature, outperforming baselines on CSI 300, CSI 1000, and S&P 500 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AlphaRLM: Aligning Language Models for Literature-Grounded Symbolic Factor Discovery
items.summary: AlphaRLM is a reinforcement-learning framework that trains large language models to construct executable symbolic factors for financial markets based on ideas extracted from financial literature, without requiring predefined factor expressions. It uses Literature-Guided Operator Assembly (LEGO) to incorporate semantic priors and aligns factor generation with market feedback through specialized reward functions. Experiments demonstrate that AlphaRLM achieves higher annualized excess returns than existing factor-mining and LLM-based methods across multiple stock indices, with an 8-billion-parameter model showing strong cross-market performance. This approach highlights the potential of combining literature conditioning and market alignment for automated factor discovery.
items.description: AlphaRLM is a reinforcement-learning framework that trains large language models to construct executable symbolic factors for financial markets based on ideas extracted from financial literature, without requiring predefined factor expressions. It uses Literature-Guided Operator Assembly (LEGO) to incorporate semantic priors and aligns factor generation with market feedback through specialized reward functions. Experiments demonstrate that AlphaRLM achieves higher annualized excess returns than existing factor-mining and LLM-based methods across multiple stock indices, with an 8-billion-parameter model showing strong cross-market performance. This approach highlights the potential of combining literature conditioning and market alignment for automated factor discovery.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.14959v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Formulaic alpha mining seeks to discover executable expressions that capture predictive market signals in a vast, noisy search space. Recent LLM-based approaches use prompting, iterative search, or seed-factor evolution, leaving direct factor construction through policy learning less explored. To address this, we introduce AlphaRLM, a reinforcement-learning framework that trains LLMs to construct executable symbolic factors from financial literature without input factor expressions. AlphaRLM incorporates Literature-Guided Operator Assembly (LEGO), which conditions factor construction on literature-derived ideas and executable operators, providing semantic priors for exploration. It further aligns the generation policy with market feedback through executable-validity and grouped-return-separation rewards that capture non-monotonic structures across factor quantiles. Extensive experiments on CSI 300, CSI 1000, and S&P 500 show that AlphaRLM outperforms strong factor-mining and LLM-based baselines in annualized excess return. Notably, the 8B model achieves strong cross-market performance, highlighting the promise of literature-conditioned, market-aligned factor generation.

items.title: Researchers introduce RELAY, a selective self-distillation method with adaptive teacher retirement for rubric-based reinforcement learning, improving performance across multiple domains [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: RELAY: Selective Self-Distillation with Adaptive Hand-off for Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning
items.summary:
RELAY addresses limitations in rubric-based reinforcement learning, where collapsing multiple criteria into a single reward loses detail and stalls learning when responses tie. The method combines selective distillation from a frozen teacher model with group reward policy optimization (GRPO), using a plateau detector to decide when to retire the teacher and continue training with GRPO alone. RELAY was calibrated on one model-domain pair and applied unchanged to three others, consistently outperforming GRPO and other methods in all settings tested.

The approach selects rollouts with positive or low zero advantages for distillation and monitors distillation loss to adaptively remove the teacher between training steps 122 and 171. Experiments on the RaR-Medicine dataset with Qwen3 models showed RELAY improved scores by 4.62 to 6.02 points over GRPO. Additionally, removing the teacher from a shared checkpoint outperformed strategies that kept, weakened, or refreshed it, and distilling selected rollouts covering about half the response tokens yielded better results than distilling all rollouts with matched coefficients.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.17623v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Rubric-based reinforcement learning grades a response against many written criteria but collapses them into one reward, which discards the detail the rubric carries and gives no GRPO reward gradient when a group's responses tie. A frozen teacher that reads the rubric as privileged context provides token-level supervision, but we observe an early plateau in the gains over GRPO. RELAY uses advantages and rewards to select positive-advantage and low-scoring zero-advantage rollouts, and monitors the distillation loss to decide when to retire the teacher. Stage 1 combines selective distillation from a frozen teacher with GRPO; a plateau detector then removes the teacher, and Stage 2 continues with GRPO alone. Calibrated on one model-domain pair and reused unchanged in three others, the plateau detector fires between steps 122 and 171. RELAY scores highest in-domain among the compared methods in all four settings, ahead of GRPO on RaR-Medicine by 4.62 points with Qwen3-1.7B and 6.02 with Qwen3-4B. On Qwen3-1.7B/Medicine, removing the teacher from a shared checkpoint outperforms keeping, weakening or refreshing it. Distilling selected rollouts covering about half the response tokens also outperforms distilling all rollouts at a matched average coefficient.

items.title: Researchers show readout scaling affects sparse autoencoder learning and propose readout-canonicalized decision-space coordinates to improve sparse feature recovery [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Readout Scaling Shapes Sparse Feature Recovery
items.summary:
Researchers investigate how readout scaling influences what sparse autoencoders learn and demonstrate that removing readout scaling benefits depend on the data distribution. They introduce readout-canonicalized decision-space (RC-DS) coordinates to eliminate singular-value gains while preserving decision information, improving sparse-factor recovery significantly compared to centered-logit training under fixed conditions.

The study includes controlled coordinate-matching experiments showing highest recovery when training matches the factor generation space. RC-DS also enhances logit reconstruction in neural policies and outperforms centered-logit SAEs in gain-free reconstruction across multiple language-model checkpoints and task sparsity settings. The findings highlight how readout scaling, data distribution, and training interact to shape sparse learning and provide a method to study and control readout contributions separately from task-specific feature usefulness.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26277v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Sequential user behavior modeling is widely adopted in industrial recommender systems; however, significant gaps remain in financial services, where pre-login web interactions and authenticated in-app experiences differ drastically. Specifically, pre-login web users typically explore new products, whereas logged-in app users focus on account servicing. Due to the challenge of cross-channel entity resolution (e.g., matching anonymous web sessions to authenticated mobile accounts), web-based intent signals remain underutilized for post-authentication personalization. Existing methods for capturing web-based intent are often ad-hoc and narrow, lacking the flexibility to support both quantitative downstream recommendations and qualitative understanding at scale. In this work, we propose a scalable and dual-purpose intent prediction framework for web-based interactions and demonstrate its applicability for personalization. Our approach transforms raw web clickstreams into two outputs: a self-supervised Transformer encodes multi-modal clickstreams into a compact session embedding, while an LLM-based taxonomy generation and distillation pipeline produces interpretable intent labels. Our system demonstrates that self-supervised clickstream representations combined with LLM-distilled taxonomies can jointly serve quantitative tasks and qualitative understanding in production: on the mobile homepage tile ranking task, the session embedding improves macro Recall@1 by 1.88% and reduces Log Loss by 13.38% over production baselines. On the user conversion prediction task, the embedding outperforms the LLM labels by 4.3% on micro F1, while the distillation layer delivers interpretable labels at ultra-low latency with only a 7% performance drop.

items.title: Researchers introduce TasteBench, a benchmark designed to measure expert-aligned taste across visual, brand, book, and tech items while addressing test-gaming artifacts and difficulty ceilings [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: How to Build a Benchmark That Actually Measures Taste
items.summary:
Researchers present TasteBench, a pairwise good-vs-bad benchmark aimed at evaluating expert-aligned taste judgments in various domains including visual, brand, book, and tech items. The benchmark uses a frozen rubric with expert-only gold standards and a control protocol to separate genuine craft judgment from test-gaming strategies. A Round-1 pilot involving three human experts and 250 item pairs identified three validity threats: position bias favoring one slot, lexical leakage from filename cues, and a difficulty ceiling inflating scores.

The team developed a protocol incorporating expert-only gold labels, weak-label firewalls, side randomization, filename scrubbing, and hard filters to measure and correct these artifacts. They released an evaluation harness and a side-randomization tool that effectively removed position bias. While position and leakage issues are fixable, the difficulty ceiling reflects inherent limits in the craft domains that require further attention in subsequent rounds. The study does not address engagement, era or circle conditioning, or calibration, and does not claim a state-of-the-art general taste benchmark.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.14707v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Expert-aligned "taste" benchmarks should reward craft judgment, not the ability to game the test. We introduce TasteBench, a pairwise good-vs-bad benchmark across visual, brand, book, and tech items under a frozen rubric with expert-only gold (panel n>=3; percent agreement >=0.60 primary gate; weak engagement labels train/analysis-only), together with a control protocol that separates craft judgment from test-gaming. Applying the protocol to a Round-1 pilot (primary_human_expert; three biological human experts; n=250 pairs) surfaces and quantifies three validity threats: two construction artifacts that inflate the trivial-baseline layer, and a difficulty ceiling that inflates every score. (1) Position: the preferred item is slot A with probability 0.956, so an always_item_a policy scores 0.956 (fair chance 0.5). (2) Lexical leakage: a filename token cue scores 0.912. (3) Difficulty ceiling: craft domains show near-ceiling human agreement (book/brand/tech 1.0), and even under A/B randomization (eval_assignment_seed7; gold_side_A ~0.47) all five VLM cards reach 1.0 on craft, with only visual separating (~0.84-0.91; a post-hoc hard subset, n=107, leaves craft at 1.0). The protocol (expert-only gold, a weak-label firewall, side randomization at construction, filename scrubbing, and hard filters) makes each artifact measurable and, for the two construction artifacts, correctable; we release a reference eval harness and a side-randomization tool, and show the tool removes the position skew (0.916 to 0.495/0.505). The result is a calibrated view of what the benchmark does and does not yet measure: position and leakage are fixable, whereas the craft-domain ceiling is a pair-difficulty limit that Round-2 must address. We do not evaluate engagement, era/circle conditioning, or calibration here, and we claim no general taste SOTA.

items.originalTitle: SuperAI: Merging Capabilities Across Heterogeneous Foundation Models
items.summary:
Researchers have developed SuperAI, a multi-model fusion framework designed to integrate complementary capabilities from diverse foundation models into a single host model. The approach uses orthogonal alignment of low-dimensional task-relevant representations and trains a lightweight residual multilayer perceptron to inject input-dependent increments, enabling scalable AI system development despite architectural differences.

SuperAI extracts task-relevant representations from source and host models using shared anchor samples and applies principal component analysis to create aligned functional subspaces. Experiments across three host models and 15 capability domains show that SuperAI outperforms existing cross-architecture fusion methods, preserving general capabilities as the number of source models increases. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of its orthogonal alignment, nonlinear residual mapping, and joint supervision components.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.15322v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Enabling the reuse and composition of knowledge and capabilities distributed across foundation models is an important step toward building scalable artificial intelligence (AI) systems. However, architectural differences and incompatible representations make it difficult to transfer and integrate these capabilities through a unified cross-model interface. To address this challenge, we propose SuperAI, a cross-architecture multi-model fusion framework that integrates complementary capabilities from multiple source models into a host model through orthogonal alignment of low-dimensional task-relevant representations. Specifically, we first extract task-relevant representations from the source models and the host model using shared anchor samples, and apply principal component analysis (PCA) to construct low-dimensional functional subspaces with the same dimensionality. Next, we use orthogonal Procrustes mappings to align the source and host coordinate systems, establishing cross-model correspondences while preserving the internal geometry of each source subspace. Finally, we train a lightweight residual multilayer perceptron (MLP) with joint supervision on task outputs and source-model increments, learning input-dependent residual increments that are injected into the host model for multi-model capability fusion. Experiments on three host models across 15 capability domains show that SuperAI achieves higher average domain scores than the evaluated cross-architecture fusion methods and better preserves general capabilities as the number of source models increases. Ablation studies further support the effectiveness of orthogonal alignment, nonlinear residual mapping, and joint supervision.

items.title: Researchers propose PASP method combining multi-perceptual views and adversarial self-play to improve detection of disguised harmful content in language models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Hidden in Plain Sight: Advancing Harmful Content Understanding via Perception-Aware Adversarial Self-Play
items.summary:
Large Language Models (LLMs) often fail to detect harmful intent hidden through deliberate obfuscation that humans can interpret using contextual, phonetic, and visual cues. To address this, researchers developed PASP (Perception-Aware Adversarial Self-Play), which integrates textual, phonetic, and visual representations of inputs and uses adversarial self-play to train models to recognize harmful intent despite evolving evasions.

PASP trains an attacker to generate intent-preserving evasions and a defender to maintain intent understanding across altered surface forms using an intent-invariance reward. Experiments demonstrate that PASP reduces adaptive attack success rates by over 70% on benchmarks like ChineseHarm-Bench and EvoHarmBench, preserves model capabilities with minimal degradation, and effectively interprets real-world evasive expressions in e-commerce contexts.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.15449v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Despite significant advances in language understanding, Large Language Models (LLMs) can still miss meaning hidden in plain sight, failing to identify harmful intent in expressions readily understood by humans. Malicious users exploit this gap by strategically disguising harmful content to evade automated moderation, posing a serious threat to online platform safety. The vulnerability reflects a fundamental cognitive asymmetry between human readers, who integrate contextual, phonetic, and visual cues to decipher the intent behind deliberate obfuscation, and text-based LLMs, which rely primarily on token sequences and have limited exposure to evolving evasions. To bridge this asymmetry, we propose PASP (Perception-Aware Adversarial Self-Play), which combines multi-perceptual views with adversarial self-play to improve understanding of harmful intent as evasions evolve. Specifically, PASP constructs textual, phonetic, and visual views of each input, preserving its original context while exposing pronunciation and glyph cues obscured in token space. During adversarial self-play, an attacker uses defender feedback to generate intent-preserving evasions, while the defender is trained using an intent-invariance reward to understand harmful intent across changing surface forms. Extensive experiments show that PASP reduces adaptive attack success rates by up to 73.71% and 74.49% on ChineseHarm-Bench and EvoHarmBench, respectively, preserves model capabilities with minimal degradation, and effectively interprets real-world evasive expressions in e-commerce.

items.title: Researchers introduce REVEAL, a training-free framework to reverse engineer agentic latents from frontier LLM model traces for local control in smaller agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: REVEAL: Reverse Engineering Agentic Latents from Frontier-Model Traces
items.summary: Researchers present REVEAL, a method that uses textual trajectories from large language model (LLM) agents to extract reusable local controls without retraining or source model access. The approach identifies agentic latents—anchored states and dynamic feedback-response profiles—by comparing successful and failed task rollouts to steer frozen target agents. Evaluations on benchmarks Terminal-Bench 2.1 and Humanity's Last Exam show improved accuracy across three target models, supported by representation analyses and behavioral case studies demonstrating the reuse of frontier-model experience as local activation control.
items.description: Researchers present REVEAL, a method that uses textual trajectories from large language model (LLM) agents to extract reusable local controls without retraining or source model access. Evaluations on benchmarks Terminal-Bench 2.1 and Humanity's Last Exam show improved accuracy across three target models, supported by representation analyses and behavioral case studies demonstrating the reuse of frontier-model experience as local activation control.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.16288v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Frontier LLM agents perform complex interactive tasks, but their inference costs motivate transferring their experience to smaller open-source agents. Distillation and latent communication typically require target-model training or access to source-model internals. We study how textual frontier-model trajectories can provide reusable local controls for a frozen agent. Inspired by protocol reverse engineering, we introduce $\textit{Agentic Latents}$, comprising anchored states and dynamic profiles of feedback--response cycles elicited by replay in the target model. Our training-free framework, $\textbf{REVEAL}$ ($\textbf{REV}$erse $\textbf{E}$ngineering $\textbf{A}$gentic $\textbf{L}$atents), uses these profiles and trajectory outcomes to match and select local events from successful and failed rollouts of the same task and source model. Their response-transition contrasts yield a target-specific steering direction, applied before each response. items.originalTitle: ResearchFlow-Eval: Tracing the Execution Gap in End-to-End Multi-Claim Autoresearch
items.summary: ResearchFlow-Eval is a new evaluation framework designed to measure continuous scientific research workflows in autoresearch systems, focusing on multiple interdependent claims and iterative revisions. It uses stage-specific rubrics derived from published anchor papers to score each research stage and assess experimental execution in detail. The framework was applied to various systems, including general-purpose agent harnesses and skill-augmented setups, revealing that experimental execution consistently lags behind design and planning stages. Systems struggled to produce high-quality results and meet claim requirements, with repeated attempts rarely improving outcomes. Neither skill augmentation nor research-specific orchestration reliably improved scores. This work extends autoresearch evaluation beyond isolated tasks to continuous, multi-claim workflows with iterative refinement.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.18088v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Autoresearch systems increasingly undertake entire research projects. In practice, scientific research requires systems to pursue multiple interdependent claims through a continuous, multi-stage workflow and revise experiments as evidence accumulates. Existing evaluations of autoresearch systems, however, typically score isolated tasks or final artifacts, leaving these process-level capabilities largely unmeasured. We therefore introduce ResearchFlow-Eval, a fine-grained framework for assessing continuous scientific execution and iteration at both the stage and claim levels. Each evaluation is grounded in a published anchor paper, from which we derive stage-specific rubrics that decompose each research stage into dimensions and separately scored rubric items. Using these rubrics, we score each research stage and examine experimental execution in detail, focusing on multi-claim completion and revisions across attempts. We apply the evaluation framework to general-purpose agent harnesses, skill-augmented harnesses, and systems with research-specific orchestration. Across all evaluated systems, experimental execution consistently lags behind design and planning. Within execution, systems struggle to produce high-quality results and meet claim requirements, and repeated attempts rarely yield measurable improvements. Moreover, neither skill augmentation nor research-specific orchestration reliably yields higher scores. ResearchFlow-Eval thus extends autoresearch evaluation beyond isolated, single-objective runs to continuous workflows in which systems pursue multiple claims and refine their work across iterations.

items.title: Researchers introduce CarryOn, an object-oriented context runtime for long-horizon agents that organizes task continuation around reusable objects, improving efficiency and reducing token usage [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Pack Light, CarryOn: Building Object-Oriented Context for Long-Horizon Agents
items.summary: Researchers present CarryOn, a new object-oriented context runtime designed for long-horizon agents that organizes continuation around reusable task objects instead of interaction histories. This approach builds context from continuation carriers, execution context, and recent interactions, maintaining validity without reconstructing full histories at each update. Experiments on OSWorld 2.0 and BrowseComp-Plus demonstrate performance gains of 5.8% and 7.0%, respectively, while reducing token usage by up to 51.9%. CarryOn offers a more efficient method for managing persistent task state in AI agents over extended interactions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.18784v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Long-horizon agents accumulate progress in persistent task state, yet repeatedly process interaction histories describing how that progress was achieved. This raises a natural question: can long-horizon context instead be organized around reusable progress rather than the history that produced it? In this paper, we introduce CarryOn, an object-oriented context runtime that organizes continuation around reusable task objects. Rather than treating compressed histories or reconstructed accounts of progress as the primary basis for continuation, CarryOn builds a context view from continuation carriers, complementary execution context, and a live tail of recent interactions. A core challenge is keeping this reusable basis valid after its surrounding history is retired: how can CarryOn update the basis without reconstructing the full representation at every fold? CarryOn maintains carrier records across folds, revising affected records against bound evidence and applicable environment checks while carrying forward unaffected records and jointly updating execution context. Experiments on OSWorld 2.0 and BrowseComp-Plus show improved gains of 5.8% and 7.0% while reducing total token usage by 51.9% and 22.9%, respectively. Project page: https://ethannju.github.io/carryon

items.title: Researchers introduce Scenario-Actor framework to adapt LLM decoding temperature based on inferred communicative scenarios, improving performance on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Read the Room Before Your Model Generates
items.summary:
Researchers propose Scenario-Actor, a temperature selection framework for large language models that adjusts decoding randomness by extracting scenario-relevant structures from Transformer hidden states to form a geometric representation of the communicative setting. This approach contrasts with traditional fixed or heuristic temperature settings by adapting to situational characteristics.

Empirical tests on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct show that Scenario-Actor enhances goal completion in interactive social scenarios, improves open-ended instruction following, and delivers competitive results in multi-turn conversations compared to existing baselines.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.18820v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) generally rely on sampling temperature to regulate the amount of randomness in their outputs. Mainstream methods for selecting temperature typically involve fixed, heuristic global settings and context or token-level calibration, rather than a geometrically interpretable representation of the communicative scenario. In this work, we introduce a simple and interpretable temperature selection framework, the Scenario-Actor, which adapts decoding to the inferred situational characteristics. Scenario-Actor extracts scenario-relevant structures from Transformer hidden states and determines the temperature from scenario embedding, a structured geometric representation of the communicative setting. Empirical results show that on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Scenario-Actor achieves strong goal-completion performance in interactive social scenarios, significant gains on open-ended instruction following, and competitive performance on multi-turn conversation compared to multiple baselines.

items.originalTitle: MvFFN: Multi-view Floor plan Feed-forward Network for Unposed Wide-Baseline Panorama Layout Reconstruction
items.summary: Researchers introduce MvFFN, a model that predicts local wall segments from wide-baseline panoramas to reconstruct accurate multi-room floor plans and camera poses without prior pose information. The approach uses Multi-view Ordered Wall Instance Segmentation (MOIS) to generate local wall predictions, which are aggregated into global layouts through a Layout Chaining post-processing pipeline. The method outperforms prior techniques in wall and junction accuracy and is supported by the new ZInD-CrossView dataset, which provides unique wall instances and cross-view segmentation labels for evaluation.

The approach uses Multi-view Ordered Wall Instance Segmentation (MOIS) to generate local wall predictions, which are aggregated into global layouts through a Layout Chaining post-processing pipeline. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.14315v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reconstructing accurate camera poses and floor-plan layouts from sparse, unposed, wide-baseline RGB panoramas remains a challenging open problem. Direct multi-room floor-plan prediction is especially difficult in this setting: pose, geometry, semantics, and global layout structure are tightly coupled, yet a complete floor-plan is hard to learn as a single global output. Our key insight is to keep the model's predictions strictly local. Multi-view Ordered Wall Instance Segmentation (MOIS) is designed around this concept. Each panorama column predicts only the wall it observes plus the next two adjacent walls in clockwise order. The global wall partition, room layouts, and shared coordinates emerge from deterministic aggregation of overlapping local predictions. Building on MOIS, we propose Multi-view floor-plan Feed-Forward Network (MvFFN), which jointly predicts coarse camera poses, dense global geometry, and per-wall semantic outputs. A downstream Layout Chaining (LC) post processing pipeline then assembles these predictions into multi-room floor-plans with shared global coordinates, consistent wall identities, and connected room structure. The dense MOIS predictions recover cross-view wall identity and local within-room connectivity more accurately than composed modular baselines, and the assembled layouts substantially outperform prior methods on wall and junction level accuracy. We also introduce the ZInD-CrossView dataset, which augments ZInD with globally unique wall instances and cross-view segmentation labels for this task.

items.title: Researchers find natural code transformations can confuse AI agents in vulnerability analysis, reducing their success in discovering software flaws [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Natural Code Transformation Confuses Agents in Vulnerability Analysis
items.summary:
Researchers studied how AI agents used for automated vulnerability discovery produce varying results on real-world code commits that have identical functionality and vulnerabilities. They found that natural, functionality-preserving code transformations derived from common software development patterns can effectively confuse these agents, such as Codex with GPT-6 Sol, lowering their success rates in vulnerability detection.

The team built a corpus of natural code transformations by mining recurring development patterns and tested their impact on agentic vulnerability analysis across multiple code domains and vulnerability categories. They also explored different types of agent failures, the potential for combining transformations to enhance protection, and how adaptive attackers might attempt to reverse these defenses. This work expands the research on using code transformations as a defense mechanism against malicious AI agents targeting software systems.

The team built a corpus of natural code transformations by mining recurring development patterns and tested their impact on agentic vulnerability analysis across multiple code domains and vulnerability categories. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.14350v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Having demonstrated a strong potential for automating vulnerability discovery, AI agents can also be used to attack software systems at scale. Today's software systems need mechanisms to level the playing field by slowing down potential attacks, giving them time to patch vulnerabilities and strengthen software. Along this line, our study of agent trajectories in vulnerability analysis shows a surprising finding: agents produce dramatically different results across real-world code commits that carry the same functionality and the same vulnerability. This phenomenon appears consistently in multiple code domains and vulnerability categories. It motivates us to study natural and functionality-preserving code transformations derived from real-world software development, and their potential as a defense against attacker agents. We build a corpus of natural transformations by mining recurring development patterns from real-world code commits, and apply them to evaluate impact on agentic vulnerability analysis. Our results show that even a single form of transformation can effectively "confuse" frontier agents, e.g., Codex with GPT-6 Sol, reducing successes in vulnerability discovery. We also study different agent failures, whether transformations can be composed to provide stronger protection, and adaptive attackers who seek to reverse them. Overall, our study of natural code transformation significantly expands the research space of using code transformations to defend against malicious agents.

items.title: RealityBench evaluates vision-language models on simulated physical work tasks across 11 environments, assessing documentation and image acceptability capabilities [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: RealityBench: Simulated Environments to Evaluate a Vision Language Model's Ability to Document Human Physical Work
items.summary:
Researchers developed RealityBench, a set of simulated environments in Blender to test vision-language models' ability to document human physical work and judge image acceptability as proof-of-work. They evaluated 26 models on tasks involving unconstrained, high-variance field work such as rooftop solar installation and vehicle repair, focusing on understanding task-relevant states and determining if views are suitable for documentation.

The study found that top models perform well when documentation answers are visible text but struggle with reading measurements and assessing small parts or spatial relations. Image acceptability proved challenging due to human rater disagreement, with models performing comparably to individual human raters. Model rankings on simulated images also transferred to real-world images for select documentation questions, indicating potential for practical application.

They evaluated 26 models on tasks involving unconstrained, high-variance field work such as rooftop solar installation and vehicle repair, focusing on understanding task-relevant states and determining if views are suitable for documentation.

The study found that top models perform well when documentation answers are visible text but struggle with reading measurements and assessing small parts or spatial relations. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.14397v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Augmenting worker capabilities in the physical world through guidance has been a decades-long goal for AI agents. One key supporting capability is to understand what the worker is doing, seeing through the human's camera or smart glasses, and assist them in documentation. Despite advances in vision language models, their capabilities in these settings remain uncertain and are challenging to benchmark because most physical work data is proprietary, and involves too much variability to study in a principled manner. Unlike structured settings such as kitchens and warehouses that have predictable lighting, geometry, and objects, field-facing tasks such as rooftop solar installation and vehicle repair are unconstrained and high variance. Here, we model real-world physical work in Blender across eleven environments, incorporating variants in both image acceptability and documentation. The acceptability task asks whether a particular view would be suitable proof-of-work and documentation asks whether an agent can understand the task-relevant state of the environment from that view. Across 26 vision-language models, we find that top models largely solve documentation when the answer is text in frame, but are weak at reading measurements and at judging small parts and spatial relations, such as whether a tape measure leans. Acceptability is harder to pin down because human raters disagree with each other. Measured against a scorer that agrees with the raters' majority about as often as a single rater does, the best models cannot be distinguished from a single non-author rater, at a cost within the range of a human pass. In the three environments where we can trace acceptability errors, most wrong rejections come from misreading the scene rather than the requirement. On the three documentation questions for which we have real images, model rankings on rendered frames transfer to real images.

Researchers developed RealityBench, a set of simulated environments in Blender to test vision-language models' ability to document human physical work and judge image acceptability as proof-of-work. They evaluated 26 models on tasks involving unconstrained, high-variance field work such as rooftop solar installation and vehicle repair, focusing on understanding task-relevant states and determining if views are suitable for documentation.

The study found that top models perform well when documentation answers are visible text but struggle with reading measurements and assessing small parts or spatial relations. Image acceptability proved challenging due to human rater disagreement, with models performing comparably to individual human raters. Model rankings on simulated images also transferred to real-world images for select documentation questions, indicating potential for practical application.

items.title: Researchers find that reviewing answers with a weaker LLM rarely outperforms the stronger model alone, highlighting anchoring effects and higher costs in verification pipelines [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Review Rarely Beats the Stronger Model: Separating Verification from Capability Transfer in LLM Pipelines
items.summary: A study comparing 48 pairs of open-weight language models from 3B to 72B parameters across math, knowledge, code, and reasoning tasks shows that review processes where a weaker model evaluates a stronger model's answers improve accuracy in only 9 of 96 cases. The researchers distinguish between verification, which genuinely adds accuracy beyond either model alone, and capability transfer, where a stronger reviewer simply supplies answers it could have generated independently. They find that reviewers tend to anchor on the generator's answers, often discarding their own correct responses, leading to diminished performance and increased computational costs—reviewing costs 2.6 to 2.8 times more than using the stronger model alone. The study suggests that verification research should report results relative to the stronger model alone rather than just gains over the generator.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.15897v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Qwen3-8B reviewing Llama-3.1-8B in math adds 33.2 points, yet Qwen3-8B alone is 6.4 points more accurate than the result. Reviewing another model's answer is usually judged by its gain over the generator. We show that this confuses verification, which adds accuracy beyond either model alone, with capability transfer, where a stronger reviewer supplies answers it could have given on its own. Measured against the stronger model alone, across 48 pairs of 12 open-weight models (3B to 72B) in math, knowledge, code and reasoning, review beats it in only 9 of 96 review directions, and does worse the larger the capability gap. The reason is anchoring: the reviewer mostly follows the generator, discarding its own correct answers. Review costs 2.6 to 2.8 times as much as the stronger model alone, while a selector using the same two calls is 2.7 to 4.2 points more accurate than review and cheaper. Studies of verification should report the stronger model alone, not only the gain over the generator.

items.title: Researchers develop a unified deep learning framework for seizure classification integrating heterogeneous EEG and intracranial EEG signals using multimodal harmonization and data augmentation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Towards Modality-Agnostic Seizure Classification: A Unified Deep Learning Framework for Heterogeneous EEG and Intracranial EEG Signals
items.summary:
Researchers present a new deep learning framework called Unified Multimodal Signal Harmonization (UMSH) that integrates heterogeneous EEG and intracranial EEG (iEEG) recordings for seizure classification. The framework addresses varied sampling rates and recording conditions and uses a Conditional Generative Adversarial Network (cGAN) to balance class distribution by generating synthetic samples. It employs EEGNet-Vision Transformer (EEGNet-ViT) for feature extraction and classification, capturing both local and global patterns in multimodal seizure data.

The study highlights the limitations of existing single-modal seizure prediction systems and emphasizes the potential of combining EEG and iEEG data to improve robustness and specificity in epilepsy monitoring. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this multimodal approach, suggesting its promise for advancing clinical decision-support systems in epilepsy treatment.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.16596v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Seizure prediction and detection, essential for clinical treatment of epilepsy, remain the crucial task of this neurological disease. EEG and iEEG are widely used to analyze epilepsy due to its capability of capturing discriminative brain activities at high time resolution. However, existing works generally analyze either EEG or iEEG seizure activity separately, where EEG analysis has been well-researched, while more and more works consider iEEG for its higher specificity at the spatial level and signal quality. Currently, most of the existing seizure prediction systems are single-modal in nature, which limits its application to a variety of clinical conditions. Therefore, a common framework to analyze seizures with both EEG and iEEG signals needs to be developed. This paper presents a new framework of multimodal seizure classification integrating the heterogeneous EEG and iEEG recordings from different subjects and sources. A specific framework, called Unified Multimodal Signal Harmonization (UMSH), is developed for harmonizing signals with varied sampling rates and recording conditions. Moreover, to handle the extremely class-imbalanced problem in the data sets, we use a Conditional Generative Adversarial Network (cGAN) based data augmentation technique to generate synthetic samples to balance the class distribution. The proposed framework uses the EEGNet-Vision Transformer (EEGNet-ViT) as the feature extraction and classification network to learn the local discriminative patterns as well as global contextual information in the multimodal seizure data. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework for robust seizure classification, emphasizing the potential of integrated EEG-iEEG multimodal learning in advancing next-generation epilepsy monitoring and clinical decision-support systems.

items.title: Cross-View Time-Frequency Diffusion for Extreme-Aware Time-Series Generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Cross-View Time-Frequency Diffusion for Extreme-Aware Time-Series Generation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.17407v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Generating realistic time-series requires faithfully reproducing rare but high-impact extreme events. Existing approaches often rely on specialized representations or extreme-focused training objectives, which may restrict the diversity of captured extremes or compromise overall distributional fidelity. We propose Cross-View Time-Frequency Diffusion (CrossTF), a framework that exploits discrepancies between time- and frequency-view denoisers for extreme-aware time-series generation. Our key empirical finding is extreme-sensitive cross-view asymmetry: moving along the direction connecting the two views' clean-sample estimates substantially changes extreme fidelity while having limited effects on overall generation quality. We further identify a late-stage cross-view window in which this discrepancy stabilizes and cross-view adjustments have a particularly strong effect on extreme fidelity. These findings motivate a staged optimization strategy in CrossTF: after training and freezing both denoisers, it only needs to learn step-specific fusion parameters within this window using an Extreme Value Theory-based objective under an energy-distance constraint. This formulation supports interpolation between and extrapolation beyond the view-specific estimates while limiting degradation in overall generation quality. Extensive experiments on seven real-world datasets against 11 baselines show that CrossTF improves extreme fidelity by 26.1% and overall performance by 7.4% relative to the strongest baselines. These results highlight cross-view discrepancy as an effective basis for low-dimensional optimization in extreme-aware time-series generation.

items.title: SkillScreen: High-Recall Screening of Malicious Agent Skills with Decision Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SkillScreen: High-Recall Screening of Malicious Agent Skills with Decision Models
items.summary: arXiv:2610.17727v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Agent skills turn natural-language instructions into actions, creating a security challenge: legitimate automation and malicious behaviour can look deceptively similar. A practical screen must catch nearly every attack while keeping the review load manageable. We present SkillScreen, a compact decision model trained to score skill maliciousness directly from SKILL$.$md in a single forward pass. On MaliciousSkillBench, SkillScreen flags 20-25% of benign skills at 99% recall on unseen attack families, substantially fewer than the word-level classifier and prompted LLM judges tested. Under the same training protocol, it also generalizes better than a fully fine-tuned encoder to unseen sources. Yet unfamiliar benign sources sharply increase false positives, showing that recognizing new attacks does not ensure reliable screening of new skill collections. Our results demonstrate the value of task-trained decision models for high-recall skill screening. Project page: https://jerroldh.github.io/SkillScreen-webpage/

items.title: MMTA: Benchmarking Multimodal Temporal Analysis with Time Series, Text, and Vision [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: MMTA: Benchmarking Multimodal Temporal Analysis with Time Series, Text, and Vision
items.summary: arXiv:2610.17856v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Time-series analysis is increasingly studied in multimodal settings, yet most benchmarks pair temporal signals with text or with visualizations derived from the same signal. This leaves open whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can integrate time series with real-world visual evidence. We introduce MMTA (multimodal temporal analysis), a benchmark of tri-modal tasks with diverse cross-modal complementarity patterns among time series, text, and vision. MMTA spans nine domains -- robotics, autonomous driving, human action, manufacturing, AR assistance, healthcare, recommendation, finance, and climate -- under video+TS and image+TS layouts, with a 3,524-sample test split covering classification and forecasting. The benchmark standardizes heterogeneous real-world sources into a shared schema with domain-specific prompts, provenance documentation, and success-weighted metrics that penalize both wrong answers and failed generations. Evaluating eight open-source and proprietary MLLMs reveals a shared bottleneck: representing time series as text creates very long token sequences and weakens fine-grained alignment with visual evidence, especially in long-video settings. We then introduce TimeOmni-v, a multimodal LLM extension with a dedicated time-series encoder, temporal positional alignment, modality-aware token layout, and a forecasting head. TimeOmni-v improves long-video classification and time-series inference efficiency, showing that MMTA not only exposes representation and grounding failures but also motivates targeted model design.

items.title: RT-J: Large-Scale Pretraining of Relational Transformers for Context-Efficient Predictions [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: RT-J: Large-Scale Pretraining of Relational Transformers for Context-Efficient Predictions
items.summary: arXiv:2610.17867v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Foundation models for tables and relational databases are increasingly used for predictive tasks across various scientific and industrial domains. However, adapting existing models to unseen datasets requires tens of thousands of examples. Here we introduce RT-J, an 85M-parameter relational foundation model (RFM) that makes accurate predictions even with hundreds of in-context examples or fewer. To achieve this, we first assemble the Join, a large collection of 639 web-crawled databases with 6,023 LLM-generated forecasting tasks. We pretrain with long contexts of up to 8,192 database cells, using in-context examples from a novel lightweight random-walk retriever. items.title: Interaction-as-a-Judge [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Interaction-as-a-Judge
items.summary: arXiv:2610.17895v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Coding agents are tasked with producing sophisticated interactive applications such as websites, desktop applications, and games. While humans assess these applications interactively, current automated LLM evaluations primarily focus on code analysis and unit tests. This mismatch can cause LLM judges to miss failures that are immediately apparent to human users. We study Interaction-as-a-Judge, an evaluation paradigm where computer-use agents (CUAs) directly interact with an application. We demonstrate that Interaction-as-a-Judge can improve both evaluation and generation of interactive applications. To this end, we collect and release two complementary datasets: $6,858$ pairs of applications with human preferences and corresponding agent traces, and $222$ applications with human-verified requirement labels. Relative to standard non-interactive approaches, we find that Interaction-as-a-Judge improves evaluation in terms of predicting human preferences ($65.6\% \to 69.1\%$) and requirement verification ($77.0\% \to 81.6\%$). We also observe scaling benefits: across both preference alignment and requirement verification, higher-quality interactions improve performance. Finally, through both inference- and training-time experiments, we demonstrate that Interaction-as-a-Judge can also improve the quality of generated artifacts. At inference time, Interaction-as-a-Judge repairs $75.5\%$ of broken requirements within five attempts, compared to $55.4\%$ for code-only self-feedback. At training time, using Interaction-as-a-Judge as a reward signal improves win-rate over the base model by $6.7$pp while reducing both generated code length by $35.7\%$ and build failure rates by $7.2$pp compared to a code-only reward signal.

items.title: Back-Translation Still Matters: Leveraging Monolingual Data for Low-Resource Machine Translation with LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Back-Translation Still Matters: Leveraging Monolingual Data for Low-Resource Machine Translation with LLMs
items.summary: arXiv:2610.18818v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Pre-trained Large Language Model (LLMs) are effective on many tasks in zero-shot and few-shot settings. For machine translation of low-resource languages, the obvious options are few-shot prompting and fine-tuning on a small parallel set. We ask: what if moderate amounts of low-resource monolingual data are also available? We argue that, rather than continued pretraining, a more effective use of this data is the pre-LLM era technique of back-translation (BT). The current fine-tuned LLM translates monolingual sentences in each language, and the resulting pairs train it in the reverse direction. Updates on the parallel set are interleaved for stable learning. With 1K parallel pairs on Odia and Swahili, BT beats continued pretraining into the low-resource language by 7.7 to 16.4 XCOMET-XXL points in domain. With beam-decoded intermediate translations, it also beats a model with 10 time more parallel data. In-context examples retrieved from the parallel data further improve BT. We also analyze the source, quality and amount of monolingual text. Across five low-resource languages, with Hindi as a high-resource control, and two 3B backbones, BT improves translation into the low-resource language by 16 to 173% XCOMET-XXL over parallel-only fine-tuning. Blind human evaluation on Odia and Sanskrit agrees with the automatic metrics.

items.title: RoboSimStudio: An Interactive Toolkit for Human and Agent Rapid Real2Sim of Robot Manipulation Tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: RoboSimStudio: An Interactive Toolkit for Human and Agent Rapid Real2Sim of Robot Manipulation Tasks
items.summary: arXiv:2610.18835v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: It has been difficult to accurately model the physics of the interaction between a robot and the objects it manipulates, including contact mechanics, coupled contact dynamics, deformations, stiffness and friction. We present RoboSimStudio (RSS), an interactive toolkit that makes choices of solver, contact model, and physical parameters explicit and editable, allowing both humans and coding agents to quickly create and iteratively refine simulations based on observed physical behavior. We implement RSS with the open Newton physics simulation system and describe experiments with human-guided real2sim using (1) visual evaluation, (2) force-feedback and (3) agentic Real2Sim2Real. Code, video and additional information can be found on the project website: https://robosimstudio.github.io

items.title: Toward Agents That Reason About Their Computation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Toward Agents That Reason About Their Computation
items.summary: arXiv:2510.22833v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: While reinforcement learning agents can achieve superhuman performance in many complex tasks, they typically do not become more computationally efficient as they improve. In contrast, humans gradually require less cognitive effort as they become more proficient at a task. If agents could reason about their compute as they learn, could they similarly reduce their computation footprint? If they could, we could have more energy efficient agents or free up compute cycles for other processes like planning. In this paper, we experiment with showing agents the cost of their computation and giving them the ability to control when they use compute. We conduct our experiments on the Arcade Learning Environment, and our results demonstrate that with the same training compute budget, agents that reason about their compute perform better on 75% of games. Furthermore, these agents use three times less compute on average. We analyze individual games and show where agents gain these efficiencies. An interactive version of this paper is available at https://adrianorenstein.com/paper/toward-compute.

items.title: Surrogate Substitution Preserves PHI Detectability: A Multi-Detector Equivalence Study [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Surrogate Substitution Preserves PHI Detectability: A Multi-Detector Equivalence Study
items.summary: arXiv:2608.03172v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Structure-preserving de-identification replaces each detected identifier with a realistic same-type surrogate ("Anna S." -> "Maria S.") rather than a tag such as [NAME]. If downstream PHI detectors no longer recognise surrogates, hiding-in-plain-sight protection and second-pass safety nets weaken. We ask: on the spans a de-identifier actually replaced, do detectors find the surrogate as often as the original value? We call this detectability preservation and treat it as a proxy, not a full measure of utility. Our paired protocol (i) scores detectability only on replaced spans, separately from coverage; (ii) runs an identical heterogeneous detector panel on original and transformed text; and (iii) bounds the paired change with document-level cluster-bootstrap equivalence testing and posterior probabilities instead of significance tests. For one commercial transform on 7 clinical and general-PII benchmarks in 7 languages (1,750 documents, 5,333 replaced spans, 11 detectors), masked-span recall moves from 75.8% to 74.6% (90% CI of the change [-1.62, -0.82] points; posterior probability > 0.99 of lying within +/-2 points). The change reaches 2-3 points on dense Spanish and Dutch text, and replaced spans are easier to detect than unreplaced ones (+16.6 points), so the result describes the replaced population only. Coverage is a separate, weaker axis (48% of gold PHI on MEDDOCAN). On financial, legal and enterprise text (750 documents, 10 detectors) the pooled result replicates (72.4% -> 72.8%), but rule-based and fine-tuned detectors lose 2-4 points on finance, and the transform edits substantial non-PII text. Redaction and Faker baselines give reference points. We release per-span predictions and analysis code.

items.title: On the Dynamics of Delayed Generalization in Linear Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: On the Dynamics of Delayed Generalization in Linear Models
items.summary: arXiv:2602.08302v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Delayed generalization, where training accuracy becomes nearly perfect substantially before test accuracy, has often been studied in the context of the depth and compositional structure of deep networks. In this paper, we ask whether delayed generalization can occur in simpler settings. We show that it can arise in a linear model trained with gradient descent and an exponential-tail loss on linearly separable data. We characterize the finite-time hyperplane dynamics into three phases: a population phase, a support vector dominated unlearning phase and a generalization phase. The convergence of the residual beyond the maximum-margin direction is sufficient for the unlearning phase to begin. In the support vector dominated phase, we characterize the hyperplane dynamics. The time scale in these dynamics causes delayed generalization. We validate our theory through controlled experiments varying population and support-vector distributions, and further verify the predicted bias behavior in a deep model with a single output neuron on MNIST. Our results provide a unified characterization of the asymptotic and finite-time dynamics underlying delayed generalization in linear models.

items.title: Hide and Seek: HIDE Concepts to SEEK explanations for black box models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Hide and Seek: HIDE Concepts to SEEK explanations for black box models
items.summary: arXiv:2610.13935v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Interpreting machine learning model predictions is a central challenge, particularly for black-box vision models. Concept-based attribution methods interpret models using human-understandable concepts. Existing concept-based methods can only interpret classification and regression models. They require access to model weights or large concept-annotated datasets, and most methods cannot provide image-level attribution. We propose Hide and Seek (HnS), a new method for concept-level attribution that does not require access to model weights or labeled concept datasets. HnS can interpret a wide range of vision models. Given a concept and image set, HnS retrieves concept-aligned images using a vision-language model, localizes the concept within each image, masks the localized region, and measures attribution from the change in the black-box model's output between the original and masked images. This enables faithful attribution by directly measuring the model's behavior and supporting local attributions. We validated HnS on CelebA and COCO-Stuff. Compared to existing methods, HnS showed better agreement with ground-truth attributions. We demonstrated the applicability of HnS on diverse tasks, including image captioning and satellite image segmentation, where no existing concept attribution method can be used. We provided our anonymous code in the supplementary material.

items.title: Correction Training for Diffusion Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Correction Training for Diffusion Models
items.summary: arXiv:2610.14136v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Iterative sampling in diffusion models can lead to error accumulation due to exposure bias. The denoiser is trained on real images interpolated with noise, but at inference its inputs are constructed from its own imperfect predictions from the earlier steps, something it has never seen at training time. This might be one reason diffusion models often struggle without additional help, such as CFG. We introduce a correction step for diffusion models which attempts to reduce this training-inference gap. The corrector takes the base model's prediction as input and is trained against the same ground-truth target. This makes correction an explicit learning task, with training inputs provided by the base model. During sampling, at each denoising step, we iteratively refine the denoiser's clean-sample prediction. This allows us to correct predictions at intermediate denoising steps, preventing early artifacts from persisting into the final sample. Although the corrector is trained only on predictions from the base denoiser, it can be applied repeatedly to its own outputs at inference for better results. This simple framework leads to substantial improvement in sample quality while largely preserving diversity. We evaluate our method across DiT, SiT, and JiT. Our method substantially improves upon previously reported FID scores for unguided generation and, notably, unconditional generation, where producing high-quality samples without guidance has been particularly challenging. Our method achieves performance competitive with classifier-free guidance (CFG), and combining correction with CFG further improves diversity and reduces oversaturation typical of CFG. Finally, we show that the additional inference cost of correction can be amortized by distilling the refined predictions back into the base diffusion model, retaining the quality gains without additional inference-time overhead.

items.title: How Should a Camera-First AI Agent Work? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: How Should a Camera-First AI Agent Work?
items.summary: arXiv:2610.14772v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Camera-first agents must act on the visual world as it unfolds. We argue that the central obstacle for future camera-first agents is not recognition ability - multimodal models (vision-language and live/streaming alike) generalize well through language and remain the right tool for semantic reasoning - but time. Many visual targets are ephemeral: they appear, are query-relevant, and leave within a short window. Binding memory to the same end-to-end path as reasoning means that by the time a monolithic pipeline completes, the evidence is gone. We formalize this as Ephemeral-Target Interaction (ETI) and a Perceptual Deadline Contract separating a hard memory deadline from a soft reasoning deadline, grounded in the bounded, passive nature of sensory and working memory. We propose a two-deadline architecture: an always-on, bounded, non-semantic fast path; an active remembering mechanism that commits a moment to durable memory before it is overwritten (event-driven in v1); and a deferred deliberation layer (multimodal model + tools). We instantiate the contract on real MOT17 track windows, a consistency check, and calibrate the single-path baseline from measured frontier-model latency: even a short answer takes 1.2-9.3 s, and an agentic identify-and-search longer. Answers can be late; evidence cannot be missed.

items.title: Agent-Canary-Mas: End-to-End Evaluation of Protocol Risk in Long-Horizon Multi-Agent Systems [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Agent-Canary-Mas: End-to-End Evaluation of Protocol Risk in Long-Horizon Multi-Agent Systems
items.summary: arXiv:2610.15529v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Agent-to-agent protocols allow LLM agents to discover peers, exchange results, and coordinate tool use. A locally successful protocol attack, however, may be rejected by a later agent or propagated into a consequential task decision. Measuring local exploitability alone leaves this difference unresolved and provides limited evidence about which participant caused the final outcome. We present Agent-Canary-Mas, an end-to-end evaluation system that follows protocol risk through long-horizon multi-agent tasks. It covers five risk classes and 13 subclasses across A2A, ANP, and BCS, with 975 matched malicious--benign task pairs in five business domains. A shared OpenClaw framework runs autonomous, tool-using agents under different underlying models while preserving the task and execution setup. Matched runs separate local protocol success from downstream consequences; retained evidence connects participant selection, message consumption, tool activity, and task-state changes. We further evaluate a protocol-context Guard that checks an object's authority at consequential handoffs. Across three model conditions, local attack success is frequently at or above 90%, while consequence conversion ranges from 7.1% to 100.0%. Cross-agent evidence raises macro-averaged Audit-F1 from 29.7% to 95.5%. On Finance tasks, the Guard lowers average ASR from 86.1% to 53.8% and PTCR from 65.5% to 31.2%, with a measurable completion tradeoff. These results show that protocol risk depends on how agents use exchanged objects throughout the task, and that evaluating this path supports more informative risk assessment, attribution, and defense.

items.title: Beyond Perfect Teammates: Multi-Agent Collaboration with Unreliable Colleagues [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Beyond Perfect Teammates: Multi-Agent Collaboration with Unreliable Colleagues
items.summary: arXiv:2610.16117v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: LLM-based multi-agent collaboration is increasingly used to solve complex tasks by dividing work among specialized agents and integrating complementary expertise. Yet existing systems and evaluations largely rest on an implicit perfect-colleague assumption: collaborators provide correct and complete information and respond promptly to requests. In realistic teamwork, however, collaborators may return information that does not answer the intended question, provide insufficient detail to support a decision, or fail to respond to a request. To separate task-solving competence from the ability to recover an unreliable evidence-gathering process, we introduce the Unreliable Colleagues Benchmark (UnCoBench), which organizes behavioral failures through Misaligned, Incomplete, and Missed settings. The main agent need to verify contextual correctness, diagnose information gap and track unresolved dependencies in order to obtain the correct evidence for solving the task. We also introduce a verifiable and scalable automated generation pipeline that pairs LLM-based scenario generation with executable checks of answer uniqueness and role necessity. Results across ten models show that similar reliable-setting performance can result in different robustness to unreliable evidence. Trace analysis reveals frequent omissions of corrective follow-up, and the recovery behavior involves inefficient waiting and redundant queries. These findings show that robust collaboration requires not only sound reasoning, but also targeted action to diagnose evidence failures, recover relevant information, and integrate it into decisions. Our data and source code are available at https://github.com/iNLP-Lab/UnCoBench.

items.title: EvoQuantLab: Training-Free Dual-Loop Evolution for Auditable Quantitative Research [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: EvoQuantLab: Training-Free Dual-Loop Evolution for Auditable Quantitative Research
items.summary: arXiv:2610.17130v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Automated alpha factor discovery is critical for modern quantitative research. While large language models (LLMs) have increasingly been integrated into quantitative workflows, existing agent-based approaches remain highly susceptible to severe backtest overfitting. To address this challenge, we propose EvoQuantLab, a training-free, dual-loop self-evolving framework for robust factor discovery. Instead of relying entirely on LLM generation, EvoQuantLab deploys an inner genetic-programming (GP) loop that dramatically improves token efficiency while evolving typed factor expressions under structural and diversity constraints. An outer diagnosis loop then systematically audits evidence across cycles to drive protocol-level improvements. Furthermore, our evaluation pipeline applies multi-metric validation to rigorously filter out spurious factors before deployment. Extensive out-of-sample experiments across both daily and hourly frequencies -- covering equities and cryptocurrency -- demonstrate the robustness of EvoQuantLab. Specifically, on daily CSI 500 and S&P 500 tasks, EvoQuantLab achieves leading annualized returns of 18.34% and 21.30%, consistently outperforming existing agent baselines. On high-turnover hourly cryptocurrency data, EvoQuantLab delivers a 37.91% annualized return while effectively avoiding execution collapse.

items.title: OpenDepth: Repurposing Image Editing Priors for Robust Open-World Monocular Depth Estimation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: OpenDepth: Repurposing Image Editing Priors for Robust Open-World Monocular Depth Estimation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.17610v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recently, the integration of generative priors has revolutionized Monocular Depth Estimation (MDE), achieving state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance with remarkably high data efficiency. However, although methods based on Text-to-Image (T2I) models excel in general scenes, their efficacy degrades sharply when confronted with open-world environmental perturbations, such as illumination variations and adverse weather. Since T2I priors are optimized for semantic synthesis rather than preserving pixel-level structure, they struggle to decouple geometry from appearance under severe visual shifts, easily triggering structural hallucinations. Therefore, our core insight is to model open-world depth estimation as consistent geometric inference across multi-style images, fully leveraging the powerful structure-preserving editing priors of Image-to-Image (I2I) models. Based on this, we propose OpenDepth, a robust open-world MDE framework that introduces "Intra-Domain Awareness" -- the capability to map diverse stylistic inputs sharing identical geometry into a unified latent space. To achieve this, we first align shallow features within the Diffusion Transformer (DiT) to anchor degraded observations to unified geometric representations. Additionally, we introduce a joint RGB latent reconstruction task, requiring the model to recover clean RGB information from degraded inputs. This multi-stage strategy effectively decouples environmental style interference, compelling the model to focus strictly on underlying geometric recovery. Extensive evaluations show that OpenDepth sets new SOTA records for robust zero-shot depth estimation across standard and extreme weather benchmarks, demonstrating exceptional structural integrity and adaptability.

items.title: RoTA-Bench: Evaluating 3D Spatial Reasoning through Interactive Projection Alignment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: RoTA-Bench: Evaluating 3D Spatial Reasoning through Interactive Projection Alignment
items.summary: arXiv:2610.17665v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Can vision-language models turn 2D observations into 3D understanding that supports precise action? This requires inferring object geometry, anticipating the effects of rotation, and refining actions through visual feedback. We introduce RoTA-Bench to evaluate these abilities through interactive 3D-to-2D projection alignment. Given a target silhouette, a model observes a rotated object and chooses successive rotations to recover the target projection within a limited action budget. Our automated pipeline constructs silhouette-preserving 3D objects from 2D icons and uses reversible initialization to guarantee solvability, yielding 674 tasks and a stratified 100-task test set. Empirically, we find that (i) a substantial human-model gap persists: GPT-5.6-Sol succeeds on only 17% of tasks, whereas 20 undergraduate participants collectively complete the test set four times with a 100% success rate; (ii) image-space and pose-space progress can diverge: at matched states, the model more often improves silhouette overlap while worsening pose alignment than humans (19.4% vs. 10.9%); and (iii) fine-grained control is sensitive to interaction history: removing it leaves 96.8% of the model's actions at a coarse 30-degree step size and sharply reduces observed task success. These findings highlight the challenge of converting visual evidence into precise 3D control, beyond recognizing or matching individual images.

items.title: ABot-ER: Unified Embodied Reasoning through Agentic Data-Model Co-Evolution [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ABot-ER: Unified Embodied Reasoning through Agentic Data-Model Co-Evolution
items.summary: arXiv:2610.18355v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce ABot Embodied Reasoning (ABot-ER), a unified embodied reasoning foundation model that breaks the tension between breadth and depth in embodied reasoning. Embodied intelligence demands the joint mastery of perception, planning, and execution, yet reconciling generality with specialization across this spectrum remains an open challenge. Within a single unified model, ABot-ER commands specialist-level depth across all three competencies, spanning spatial, scene, and temporal reasoning in perception; long-horizon action organization in planning; and point grounding and affordance in execution. The Agentic Data-Model Self-Evolution Engine continuously adapts data strategies to the model's evolving capability state. The Task-Conditioned Adaptive Training Strategy uses task tokens to activate lightweight low-rank residuals over a shared backbone, separating updates from heterogeneous output formats while retaining shared embodied knowledge. Across a systematic evaluation on twelve benchmarks covering three core competencies and five capability dimensions, ABot-ER achieves state-of-the-art overall performance across perception, planning, and execution within a unified parametric framework, demonstrating that breadth and depth can coexist in unified embodied reasoning.
